item.title: New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote
item.description:
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump pose for a photo at the first ever meeting of the leaders of the US, Russia and China. Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images AsiaPac/AP
View image in fullscreen
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump pose for a photo at the first ever meeting of the leaders of the US, Russia and China. Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images AsiaPac/APAnalysis
New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda
It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.
But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.
It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.
Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea, the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.

item.title: Election date? Brexit reset outcome? Farage’s survival chances? Andrew Sparrow answers your questions
item.description:
NoMoreMrNice asks:
double quotation mark
Hi Andrew - nice to have you back. Or us back, I guess. Thanks for the blog.
As someone who must follow the daily political shenanigans more than most, do you find the way it functions depressing? Less the positions or the policies, but the mechanisms of it - in particular the regular pretence that anybody from another party is absolutely wrong; that anything you disagree with is a laughable disgrace; that politicians who know very well how difficult the problems are pretend it’s just government incompetence that means they aren’t solved; and the general poverty of discourse.
I’ve been re-reading some of the speeches from around the abolition of slavery, and I just can’t imagine any modern politician reaching the same level of rhetoric, or of nuance, now. Even 20 years ago, I remember some politicians who gave cracking speeches in parliament, raising really interesting perspectives. Tony Benn was a great speaker, but I always liked Tony Wright too. Do MPs still give interesting speeches, and I just don’t see them? Or is it just me growing grumpy grumpier with age, and harking back to some prelapsarian idyll that never really existed?
If not, and you think there is an issue with the *how* of modern politics, do you see any particular causes, or any possible solutions? To me, we seem to have more public debate than ever, and nearly all of it seems almost entirely banal and pointless.
Until now, I have been choosing questions where I felt reasonably well qualified to give an answer. I posted this one because it is interesting and challenging; I’m not sure I do have an answer, but here goes anyway.
Years ago I wrote a book that involved reading 19th century debates and, I agree, they require a level of concentration that would be beyond most parliamentarians, or listeners, now. But that parliamentary debate was an elite activity, it was a pre-democratic age, and there was no TV.

item.description:

View image in fullscreen
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the trilateral talks in China. Photograph: White House Office/APAImages/Shutterstock
China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
Press conference following the end of Apec summit – watch live
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. item.title: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
item.description:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin take part in a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin take part in a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images
Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.Global courts under attack and four more takeaways from the Trump, Xi, Putin meeting
Read more
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump, California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway.
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.

item.title: Global courts under attack and four more takeaways from the Trump, Xi, Putin meeting
item.description:
Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Photograph: Kremlin Press Service/Anadolu/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Photograph: Kremlin Press Service/Anadolu/Getty Images
Global courts under attack and four more takeaways from the Trump, Xi, Putin meeting
No breakthroughs on major subjects at first trilateral summit between leaders of US, China and Russia
The presidents of the US, China and Russia met on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral gathering on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. The session lasted more than an hour and Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin touched on nuclear weapons, the war in Ukraine and wider international security.
The trio lead the world’s three major nuclear powers and their decisions have far-reaching consequences for global security. However, their meeting in China ended without an announced breakthrough or concrete agreement on the main issues. Here are five key takeaways:
Trump declared the meeting ‘historic’
Trump opened the talks by telling Xi and Putin that “we are really making history”. He described the US, China and Russia as “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles and lowering the risk of such weapons being used.
It was an unusually high-profile display of cooperation between three countries whose relations have been marked by significant tensions, especially over Ukraine, trade disputes and the Nvidia scandal.
Trump also argued that peace could not be achieved by turning down opportunities for dialogue. It was the first time the leaders of the three countries had held a trilateral summit of this kind.

item.title: In an authoritarian economy, Jensen Huang may be too big to fail | Robert Reich
item.description:
‘Even in an authoritarian economy, no CEO is above the law. Or is he?’ Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
‘Even in an authoritarian economy, no CEO is above the law. Or is he?’ Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters
In an authoritarian economy, Jensen Huang may be too big to fail Robert Reich
A handful of men control the US economy. They have leveraged themselves to be – or seem – indispensable
Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it.
“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang, who admitted being unfaithful to his wife, resigned from Nvidia last week. US intelligence agencies have identified one of his alleged lovers as a spy for China. If true, Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips may have found their way there.
Beyond the tabloid headlines lies a much bigger story – a US economy that’s become dependent on the initiatives and decisions of a few powerful men who are too big to fail.
We tend to think of government as being authoritarian, democratic or somewhere in between. For the last 22 months, we’ve witnessed what happens when the US government turns authoritarian.
An economy can also be described along the same continuum.
Throughout most of the last century, the US economy was fairly democratic. Decisions about what was produced and at what price reflected the judgments of tens of thousands of corporate executives, managers and small-business owners – all of whom were trying to respond to consumers and investors. item.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
item.description:
The Markley Lowell datacentre in Lowell, Massachusetts. The US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. Photograph: Lauren Owens Lambert/AFP/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
The Markley Lowell datacentre in Lowell, Massachusetts. The US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. Photograph: Lauren Owens Lambert/AFP/Getty Images
Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas
The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.
Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.
Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
Sanae Takaichi cuts lonely figure at airport, a move by China that is being linked to the simmering row over Taiwan
Apec’s Chinese hosts went out of their way to give world leaders a warm welcome as they arrived in Shenzhen this week. Military bands played, dozens of cheering young men and women waved colourful bouquets, and senior officials offered hugs and handshakes on the tarmac.
But there was one exception: Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.
The red carpet was rolled out for her arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport, but Takaichi, on her first visit to China since taking office just over a year ago, had to make do with a modest guard of honour and a welcome from a relatively junior Chinese government official.Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit

The contrast in hospitality was impossible to ignore. Donald Trump was personally greeted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping as he stepped off Air Force One, while Vladimir Putin was met by Cai Qi, a senior Communist party official and one of Xi’s closest aides.
The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, beamed as he walked past rows of women in white shirts and pink skirts while soldiers from the People’s Liberation Army stood to attention, bayonets fixed. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, and the country’s first lady, Kim Hea Kyung, were given similar VIP treatment.

item.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
item.description:
Donald Trump greets Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping before a dinner at the Apec summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photograph: Emre Aytekin/Anadolu/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Donald Trump greets Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping before a dinner at the Apec summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photograph: Emre Aytekin/Anadolu/Getty Images
The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress Editorial
A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies
“Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.
The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.
Mr Xi looks like the power broker bringing Moscow and Washington together, and the gracious host, in a city which showcases China’s economic and technological progress and aspirations. The contrast between the glossy metropolis and a US currently beset by glaring tech failures hitting everything from flights to banking is especially flattering. For Mr Putin, who gloated about the “humiliation” of Europe in the run-up, this meeting is an even clearer win, making him look like a superpower peer rather than the leader of a pariah nation with a struggling economy.

item.description:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here

Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday.

It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe | Rafael Behr
item.description:
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours

In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power”.

Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist
